question: How do we let the association between a predictor and an outcome depend on another predictor, and how do we fit, interpret and plot such interactions?
contributions: Builds a linear interaction by making a slope its own linear model
Triptych plots and centering for continuous interactions

limits: Uses MAP quadratic approximation (map), not MCMC; the chapter says it needs a more capable conditioning engine in the next chapter
Flat/weak priors on tulips; author says flat priors are not the best thing to do
Only 27 tulip rows; interaction for Africa rests on few African countries (dSE nearly equals dWAIC between m7.5 and m7.4)
WAIC use is debated here since no one resamples nations; author says reasonable people disagree
Bed (cluster) variable left out of tulip analysis; deferred to exercise 7H1
Linear interactions are only a descriptive epicycle; a mechanistic model would be better (author)
First-edition rethinking/map code, dated against ulam/quap
practices: Do not split data by group to get different slopes; model the split inside one model so sigma is shared and uncertainty on the grouping is quantified (p.213-214)
Do not read an interaction from a table of means; plot posterior predictions (p.219, p.233)
Compute any derived quantity (e.g. gamma) from posterior samples so it carries uncertainty (p.221)
Compute the distribution of a difference directly; marginal-density overlap is not a test (p.222)
Centre continuous predictors: the intercept becomes the grand mean, main effects keep their meaning across models, and optimisation converges (p.225-232)
Give optimiser explicit start values and consider Nelder-Mead or more iterations when MAP fitting fails (p.228-230)
Use a triptych plot, fixing the other variable at several values, for continuous interactions (p.233)
Treat the two readings of a linear interaction as the same model and plot both (p.223-225)
Use non-standard interval widths (97%) to remind that 95% is arbitrary (p.215)

terms.definition: a kind of conditioning, a way of allowing parameters (really their posterior distributions) to be conditional on further aspects of the data
built by extending the linear modeling strategy to parameters within the linear model (a slope defined as a linear model)
a panel of three complementary figures that comprise a whole picture of the regression results
create a new variable that contains the same information as the original, but has a new mean of zero
